quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Clause with who
quests.questionSentence: The pharmacist ___ filled my prescription mentioned a possible side effect.
quests.completedSentence: The pharmacist who filled my prescription mentioned a possible side effect.
quests.ruleExplanation: Nothing else performs 'filled,' so 'the pharmacist' must be its subject - 'who' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Find 'filled' - does anything else in the sentence already perform that action?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: The specialist ___ my doctor recommended specializes in sports injuries.
quests.completedSentence: The specialist whom my doctor recommended specializes in sports injuries.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'My doctor' is the subject of 'recommended,' so 'the specialist' is the object being recommended - 'whom' marks this role in formal English.
quests.nativeTip: 'My doctor' already has a job in this clause - 'recommended.' What does that leave for the specialist?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with which
quests.questionSentence: The medication ___ the doctor prescribed caused an unexpected reaction.
quests.completedSentence: The medication which the doctor prescribed caused an unexpected reaction.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The doctor' is the subject of 'prescribed,' so 'the medication' is the object - a thing in that role takes 'which.'
quests.nativeTip: 'The doctor' already performs an action in this clause. What role does that leave for the medication?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The man ___ car I borrowed for the weekend was surprisingly generous.
quests.completedSentence: The man whose car I borrowed for the weekend was surprisingly generous.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' shows that the car belongs to the man; the borrowing is a separate action happening inside the clause, but the link between 'the man' and 'car' is still possession.
quests.nativeTip: Focus on 'car' - who does it belong to? That's the relationship the blank must show, even though 'I borrowed' looks like the main action.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: The man ___ I called for help was surprisingly generous.
quests.completedSentence: The man whom I called for help was surprisingly generous.
quests.ruleExplanation: Unlike the previous sentence, there's no possession here - 'I' is the subject of 'called,' and the man is the object being called, which calls for 'whom.'
quests.nativeTip: This time, check whether the blank shows ownership of something, or whether it marks the man as the one 'I called.'

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The artist ___ painting I admired for years finally agreed to an interview.
quests.completedSentence: The artist whose painting I admired for years finally agreed to an interview.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' correctly shows that the painting belongs to the artist; 'I admired' is simply the action happening inside that possessive clause.
quests.nativeTip: Look at 'painting' - it belongs to someone. Find who that is, regardless of the fact that 'I admired' is also part of the clause.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The client ___ complaint I resolved personally sent a thank-you note.
quests.completedSentence: The client whose complaint I resolved personally sent a thank-you note.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' is correct because the complaint belongs to the client; this is a possession relationship, not the client being the direct object of an action.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether the blank shows something belonging to the client, or whether it marks the client as being acted upon directly.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: The client ___ I contacted about the complaint sent a thank-you note.
quests.completedSentence: The client whom I contacted about the complaint sent a thank-you note.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I' is the subject of 'contacted,' making the client the object of that action - which calls for 'whom,' not the possessive 'whose.'
quests.nativeTip: This time, there's no possession word right after the blank - check instead who is doing the contacting.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The employee ___ manager praised her publicly felt truly valued.
quests.completedSentence: The employee whose manager praised her publicly felt truly valued.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' is correct because the manager belongs to (is the manager of) the employee; without 'whose,' the sentence would need a completely different structure to make sense.
quests.nativeTip: Check what comes right after the blank - 'manager' - and ask who that manager belongs to.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence uses the most formally correct object pronoun?
quests.targetClause: The professor whom I studied under later became a mentor.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence uses the most formally correct object pronoun?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' is the traditionally correct object pronoun for formal writing. 'Who' is extremely common in everyday speech and widely accepted informally, but 'whom' is the more formally precise choice here.
quests.nativeTip: In casual conversation, people often relax this rule - but for the most traditionally correct option, check which pronoun is built specifically to mark an object role.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The professor whom I studied under later became a mentor."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Who in Informal Register
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence would sound most natural in a casual conversation between friends?
quests.targetClause: That's the guy who I met at the gym.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence would sound most natural in a casual conversation between friends?
quests.ruleExplanation: In casual spoken English, 'who' is the overwhelmingly natural choice even in object position; 'whom' would sound stiff or overly formal between friends. 'Whose' and 'which' are simply wrong here.
quests.nativeTip: Think about how you'd actually say this out loud to a friend, rather than how you'd write it in a formal report.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "That's the guy who I met at the gym."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: In her official report, the inspector wrote: 'The technician ___ we consulted confirmed the damage was extensive.'
quests.completedSentence: In her official report, the inspector wrote: 'The technician whom we consulted confirmed the damage was extensive.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' fits the formal, written register of an official report; it correctly marks 'the technician' as the object of 'consulted.'
quests.nativeTip: This sentence comes from an official written report - check which object pronoun best matches that formal setting.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Clause with which
quests.questionSentence: The invoice ___ was sent twice by mistake still hasn't been corrected.
quests.completedSentence: The invoice which was sent twice by mistake still hasn't been corrected.
quests.ruleExplanation: There's no other subject for 'was sent,' so 'the invoice' must be it - 'which' is correct since an invoice is a thing.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'was sent' already has a subject elsewhere, or whether the gap needs to supply one.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with which
quests.questionSentence: The refund ___ the customer requested twice finally processed today.
quests.completedSentence: The refund which the customer requested twice finally processed today.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The customer' is the subject of 'requested,' so 'the refund' is the object - a thing in that role takes 'which.'
quests.nativeTip: 'The customer' already has a job in this clause. What role does that leave for the refund?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Pronoun 'that' for Things
quests.questionSentence: The delivery ___ arrived two days late upset several customers.
quests.completedSentence: The delivery that arrived two days late upset several customers.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' correctly refers to 'the delivery,' a thing, functioning as the subject of 'arrived.'
quests.nativeTip: Nothing else in the sentence performs 'arrived' - check whether the gap needs to supply that subject.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The signature on the contract ___ our legal team is still reviewing could delay the deal.
quests.completedSentence: The signature on the contract which our legal team is still reviewing could delay the deal.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Our legal team' is the subject of 'is reviewing,' so 'the signature' - not 'the contract' - is the object being reviewed; since a signature is a thing, 'which' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: 'On the contract' just tells you where the signature is - and 'our legal team' already has a job in this clause. What does that leave?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: The director of the regional branch ___ the board eventually dismissed had only started in January.
quests.completedSentence: The director of the regional branch whom the board eventually dismissed had only started in January.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The board' is the subject of 'dismissed,' so 'the director' is the object being dismissed - a person in that role takes 'whom.'
quests.nativeTip: 'Of the regional branch' just describes which director - and 'the board' already has a job in this clause. What does that leave for the director?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The founder of the small bakery ___ recipes have been passed down for generations recently retired.
quests.completedSentence: The founder of the small bakery whose recipes have been passed down for generations recently retired.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' is correct because the recipes belong to the founder, despite 'bakery' sitting closer to the gap.
quests.nativeTip: 'Of the small bakery' just tells you which founder - find what belongs to that founder.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: A company's CEO resigned, and the company announced a replacement within a week. Which sentence correctly combines these ideas?
quests.targetClause: The company whose CEO resigned announced a replacement within a week.
quests.completedSentence: A company's CEO resigned, and the company announced a replacement within a week. Which sentence correctly combines these ideas?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' correctly shows possession - the CEO belongs to the company - and works for organizations just as it does for people. The other options either misuse a contraction, an object pronoun, or a plain thing-pronoun that can't show possession this way.
quests.nativeTip: Only one option correctly shows that the CEO belongs to (leads) the company.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The company whose CEO resigned announced a replacement within a week."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: A teacher assigned a project, and students later doubted the project's usefulness. Which sentence correctly combines these ideas?
quests.targetClause: The teacher whose project students later doubted retired that year.
quests.completedSentence: A teacher assigned a project, and students later doubted the project's usefulness. Which sentence correctly combines these ideas?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' is the only pronoun here that can show possession - the project belongs to the teacher. Neither 'who' nor 'whom' can do this job, and 'which' incorrectly treats the teacher as a thing.
quests.nativeTip: Look for the option where the project clearly belongs to the teacher.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The teacher whose project students later doubted retired that year."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with which
quests.questionSentence: A developer released an update, and users had been requesting it for months. Which sentence correctly combines these ideas?
quests.targetClause: The update which users had been requesting for months finally fixed the bug.
quests.completedSentence: A developer released an update, and users had been requesting it for months. Which sentence correctly combines these ideas?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Which' correctly refers to 'the update,' a thing, functioning as the object of 'had been requesting'; the other options either wrongly personify the update or misuse possession.
quests.nativeTip: Check that the pronoun correctly marks an object role for a thing, not a person or a possessive relationship.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The update which users had been requesting for months finally fixed the bug."

quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' shows the photo belongs to the woman; 'I took' is simply the action happening within that possessive clause.
quests.nativeTip: Focus on 'photo' - who does it belong to? The fact that 'I took' it doesn't change that relationship.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun (Preview)
quests.questionSentence: The report that I finished last night impressed my manager. Which single word could be removed without making the sentence ungrammatical?
quests.completedSentence: The report that I finished last night impressed my manager. Which single word could be removed without making the sentence ungrammatical?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' can be dropped here because 'the report' is the object of 'finished,' not the subject - object relative pronouns like this are often optional in English. You'll explore this fully in upcoming levels.
quests.nativeTip: This word introduces an object relative clause - in English, this type of relative pronoun is sometimes optional. Which one is it?
